column2: He pierced Shrutakirti with nine, Sutasoma with five, Shrutakarman with eight, Pratívindhya with three arrows, Shatanika with nine, and the son of Dharma with seven.
Then he struck the other heroes with two each, and cut Shrutakirti's bow with sharp arrows.
Then the great chariot-warrior Shrutakirti, taking another bow, pierced Drona's son with three sharp arrows and again with others.
Then Drona's son, O great king, O Bharata, covered that army and the kings on every side with showers of arrows.
Then again the immeasurable-souled Drona's son, laughing, cut the king of dharma's bow and pierced him with three arrows.
Then the son of Dharma, O king, taking another great bow, pierced Drona's son with seventy and tormented his arms and chest.
Satyaki, enraged, cut Drona's son's bow as he struck in battle with a sharp half-moon arrow and roared hard.
With his bow cut, Drona's son, best of the mighty, with a dart quickly felled Shaineya's charioteer from his chariot.
Then, taking another bow, the mighty son of Drona covered Shaineya with showers of arrows, O Bharata.
His horses, when the charioteer fell, were seen running here and there, O Bharata.
Those led by Yudhishthira rushed with speed at Drona's son, best of weapon-bearers, loosing sharp arrows.
Seeing them coming, terrible in form, the scorcher of foes, Drona's son, laughing, met them in the great battle.
Then Drona's son, a great chariot-warrior blazing with hundreds of arrows, burned the army in the battle as fire burns dry grass in a forest.
That army of the sons of Pandu, scorched by Drona's son, was agitated, O best of the Bharatas, like a river's mouth by a whale.
Seeing Drona's son's prowess, O great king, they thought all the Pandavas slain by Drona's son.
Yudhishthira, swiftly embracing the great chariot-warrior Drona's son, filled with anger and indignation, said to him:

You have no affection and no gratitude, tiger among men, since today you seek to kill me alone.
mahabharata:8:39.32	A Brahmana should practise austerity, giving and study; a kshatriya should bend the bow; you are a so-called Brahmana.
mahabharata:8:39.33	Mighty-armed one, I shall conquer the Kauravas in battle before your eyes; do your deed in battle, you are surely a Brahmana in name only.
Thus addressed, O great king, Drona's son, as if smiling, reflecting that it was fitting, said nothing in reply.
Saying nothing, he covered the Pandava in battle with showers of arrows, enraged like Death among creatures.
Covered then by Drona's son, O revered one, Partha quickly withdrew, leaving the great host.
When the king of dharma Yudhishthira had retreated, Drona's son stood, O king, by the great soul's refusal.
Then King Yudhishthira, leaving Drona's son in the great battle, went to your army, bent on cruel deed.
Then Karna, enraged, slew the Chedis, Karushas and Srinjayas, great chariot-warriors, in Bhimasena's sight.
Bhimasena then left Karna, best of chariot-warriors, and went to the Kaurava army, blazing like fire in dry grass.
The charioteer's son too in the battle slew the Panchalas, Kekayas and Srinjayas, mighty archers, by thousands.
Among the Samshaptakas the Parthas, among the Kauravas Vrikodara, and among the Panchalas Karna, the great chariot-warriors made destruction.
Those kshatriyas, burning by those three like fires, went to destruction in battle through your ill counsel, O king.
Then Duryodhana, enraged, pierced Nakula with nine arrows and his four horses, O best of the Bharatas.
Then again your son, the immeasurable-souled king, cut Sahadeva's golden banner with a razor-arrow.
Nakula, enraged, struck your son with seventy-three arrows in battle, O king, and Sahadeva with five.
Then with two other broad-headed arrows he cut the twins' bows, laughing, O king, and pierced them with seven.
Those two, taking other fine bows, beautiful, like Indra's bow, shone in the battle like sons of the gods.
Then those two brothers, impetuous in battle, O king, rained dreadful arrows on their brother like two great clouds on a mountain.
Then, enraged, your son, the great chariot-warrior, held back the two mighty-bowed sons of Pandu with arrows.
Only the circle of his bow was seen in the battle, O Bharata, and arrows were seen issuing on every side.
Covered with his arrows, the two Pandavas shone dimly, like the moon and sun obscured by cloud in the sky.
Those arrows, O great king, golden-feathered and whetted on stone, covered all quarters like the rays of the sun.
When the sky was thus covered and filled with arrows, the twins' form was seen like that of Death the ender and Yama.
Seeing that prowess of your son, the great chariot-warriors thought the sons of Madri had come near to death.
Then the commander of the great-souled Pandava, the Parshata, went there where King Suyodhana was.
Then, passing the two heroic sons of Madri, the great chariot-warriors, Dhrishtadyumna struck your son with arrows.
Your very impatient son of immeasurable spirit, laughing, O best of men, pierced the Panchala with twenty-five.
Then again, O lord of the earth, your son pierced the Panchala with sixty-five and roared.
Then the king cut his bow with its arrow and his hand-guard, O revered one, with a very sharp razor-arrow in the battle.
Casting aside the cut bow, the Panchala, tormentor of Shakra, quickly took another new bow able to bear burdens.
Blazing, as it were, with impetus, his eyes red with fury, the mighty-bowed Dhrishtadyumna, though wounded, shone.
He loosed fifteen iron arrows like hissing serpents, wishing to kill the best of the Bharatas.
Piercing the king's golden armour, those stone-whetted arrows, heron-feathered, entered the earth with speed.
Deeply pierced, O great king, your son shone like a flowering kimshuka tree in spring.
With his armour cut, his skin torn by the iron arrows' blows, he, enraged, cut Dhrishtadyumna's bow with a broad-headed arrow.
Then the king, in haste, afflicted the bowless one between the brows with ten arrows, O king.
Those smith-polished arrows adorned his face like bees eager for honey on a blooming champaka.
Casting aside the cut bow, the high-minded Dhrishtadyumna swiftly took another bow and sixteen broad-headed arrows.
Then the Parshata killed Duryodhana's horses and his charioteer with five, and cut his gold-adorned bow with a broad-headed arrow.
The Parshata cut, with nine broad-headed arrows, your son's chariot with its gear, parasol, dart, sword, mace and banner.
All the kings saw the banner of the lord of the Kurus, with golden armlet, variegated, jewelled and fair, with its elephant emblem, cut down.
His brothers protected Duryodhana, chariotless and with all his weapons cut, in the battle, O best of the Bharatas.
Daṇḍadhara, bewildered, placing him on a chariot, O king, carried the lord of men away in the sight of Dhrishtadyumna.
Karna, having defeated Satyaki, hungry for the king, the mighty, rushed in battle at the slayer of Drona (Dhrishtadyumna) of fierce arrows.
Shaineya quickly followed him from behind, piercing him with arrows, like an elephant goring the rear of another with its tusks.
There was a great battle then, O Bharata, among your high-minded warriors, between Karna and the Parshata.
No warrior among the Pandavas or among us was seen turning away when Karna swiftly went against the Panchalas.
At that moment, O best of men, a destruction of elephants and horses appeared on both sides, O king, when the day was at its middle.
The Panchalas, O great king, in haste, eager for victory, rushed from all sides at Karna like birds at a tree.
Adhiratha's son, enraged, picking out with the tips of his arrows those high-spirited strivers, reached them in front:
Vyaghraketu, Susharma, Shanku, fierce Dhananjaya, Shukla, Rochamana and the invincible Simhasena.
Those heroes with the speed of their chariots surrounded the best of men, who was enraged, loosing arrows, ornament of the battle.
The glorious lord of men, Radheya, killed eight of those fighting heroes with eight sharp arrows.
Then, O great king, the glorious charioteer's son, skilled in war, slew many thousands more warriors.
He slew Vishnu and Vishnukarman, Devapi and Bhadra, Danda and Chitra, Chitrayudha and Hari in the battle, O king.
Enraged, he slew Simhaketu, Rochamana, the great chariot-warrior Shalabha, and the great chariot-warriors of the Chedis.
As Adhiratha's son took their lives, his body, with limbs drenched in blood, appeared great and mighty like Rudra's.
There, O Bharata, elephants struck by Karna's arrows ran in fear on all sides, causing great confusion.
Tormented by Karna's arrows, they fell to the ground in the battle, making sounds of many kinds, like mountains struck by thunderbolts.
With elephants, horses and men falling all around, and chariots lying on the road, the earth was strewn.
Neither Bhishma nor Drona nor others of yours in the battle did such a deed as was done in the battle.
By the charioteer's son a great slaughter was made among elephants, chariots, horses and men, O tiger among men.
As a lion is seen ranging fearless among deer, so Karna ranged fearless among the Panchalas.
As a lion drives herds of terrified deer in all directions, so Karna routed the Panchala chariot-throngs.
As deer never survive on meeting a lion's jaws, so great chariot-warriors do not survive meeting Karna.
As people burn on meeting blazing Vaishvanara fire, so in the battle the Srinjayas were burned by the fire of Karna, O Bharata.
By Karna alone among the Chedis and Panchalas many esteemed heroes were slain after proclaiming their names, O Bharata.
And it seemed to me, O lord of men, seeing Karna's prowess, that no single Panchala would escape Adhiratha's son alive in the battle.
Destroying the Panchalas in the battle, the glorious charioteer's son rushed, enraged, at Yudhishthira, son of Dharma.
Dhrishtadyumna and the sons of Draupadi, O revered one, and hundreds of others surrounded the king, slayer of foes.
Shikhandin, Sahadeva, Nakula, Nakula's son, Janamejaya, the grandson of Shini and many Prabhadrakas,
these, of immeasurable vigour, leading the way for Dhrishtadyumna in the battle, ranged around Karna as he shot with arrows and missiles.
The son of Adhiratha alone there attacked many Chedis, Panchalas and Pandavas in the battle, as Garuda attacks serpents.
Bhimasena, enraged, alone in the battle, fighting many of the Kurus, Madras and Kekayas, shone, a mighty archer.
There, struck in their vital parts by Bhima's iron arrows, elephants with riders slain fell and shook the earth.
Horses with riders slain and foot-soldiers lifeless lay in the battle, pierced through, vomiting much blood.
Thousands of chariot-warriors lay fallen with weapons fallen, seen unwounded, lifeless from fear of Bhima.
With chariot-warriors, horses, charioteers, foot-soldiers and elephants cut by Bhimasena's arrows, the earth was strewn.
That army of Duryodhana, tormented by Bhimasena's strength, stood as if paralysed, O king, dispirited and wounded.
Motionless in the tumult, wretched in that great battle, it was like the sea with calm waters in due season, O king.
That army of your son, endowed with fury, valour and strength, was by arrows brought down by force; it was drenched with floods of blood and became wet with it.
Karna, enraged in battle, with the Pandava army, and Bhimasena routing the Kurus, shone greatly.
While that dreadful, wondrous battle went on, having slain many hosts of Samshaptakas in the midst of the army,
Arjuna, best of victors, said to Vasudeva, "Janardana, this army is broken, even as it is about to fight.
These Samshaptaka great chariot-warriors run with their followers, unable to withstand my arrows, like deer from lion-roars.
The great army of the Srinjayas is torn in the great battle, and there, Krishna, is the elephant-rope banner of the wise Karna, seen ranging again and again in the middle of the king's army.
Other great chariot-warriors cannot conquer Karna in battle; you know Karna's valour in prowess.
Go there, to where Karna is routing our army.
Or avoiding the great chariot-warrior, the charioteer's son, go elsewhere in the battle. Fatigue does not trouble me, Krishna, or as it pleases you."
Hearing this, O great king, Govinda, laughing, quickly said to Arjuna, "Slay the Kauravas, Pandava."
Then, urged by Govinda, the swan-white horses entered your great army carrying Krishna and the Pandava.
With the white horses sent by Keshava adorned with gold, entering, your army was split in four directions.
Having broken the great army, Keshava and Arjuna entered, enraged, red-eyed with fury, and shone, greatly radiant.
Those two, challenged by their foes to the sacrifice of battle, were like the two Ashvins invoked at a sacrifice by sacrificers with due rite.
Those two tigers among men, enraged, became swift, like two elephants angered at the sound of palms in the great battle.
Plunging into the chariot-force and the hosts of horses, Phalguna ranged in the middle of the army like Death with a noose in hand.
Seeing him valorous in the battle, your son again urged the Samshaptaka hosts against him.
Then with a thousand chariots, three hundred elephants, fourteen thousand horses in the great battle,
and two hundred thousand famed, well-known brave bowmen on foot, the great chariot-warriors attacked those two heroes, covering them.
Covered in battle by arrows, the tormentor of hostile forces, showing a dreadful form like Death with a noose in hand, slaying the Samshaptakas, Partha became yet more terrible to behold.
Then with arrows bright as lightning, adorned with gold, the sky seemed uninterrupted, driven by Kiritin's arrows.
Covered with the great arrows flying from the arms of Kiritin, all seemed, O lord, as if full of Kadru's offspring.
The Pandava of immeasurable spirit showed, in all directions, golden-feathered, bright-tipped, straight-jointed arrows.
Having slain ten thousand kings of the Samshaptakas, the great chariot-warrior, son of Kunti, swiftly advanced on the enemy host.
Reaching the enemy host guarded by the Kambojas, Partha crushed it by force with arrows, as Vasava the danavas.
With broad-headed arrows he swiftly cut the weapon-bearing arms and heads of the aggressor foes.
With their limbs and members cut off, weaponless, they fell to the ground like many-branched trees broken on every side by wind.
As Arjuna slew throngs of elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers, the younger brother of Sudakshina rained showers of arrows on him.
As he shot, Arjuna with two half-moon arrows struck off his two arms like iron clubs, and with a razor-arrow his head, face like the full moon.
He fell from his mount, streaming his own blood, like a peak of a mountain of realgar split by a thunderbolt.
They saw the Kamboja, younger brother of Sudakshina, slain: tall, lotus-eyed, very handsome, like a golden pillar, like a golden mountain split.
Then there was again a dreadful, wondrous battle, and the warriors fighting there showed many conditions.
With the Kamboja, Yavana and Shaka horses turned about, everything became red, drenched with blood, O lord of men.

With chariots, horses, charioteers and horses with riders slain, elephants with riders slain, and chief officers of slain elephants, a dreadful destruction of men was made by one another, O great king.
While that enemy host was being slain by the great soul, Drona's son quickly came against Arjuna, best of victors.
Shaking his great bow adorned with gold, taking dreadful arrows, as the sun takes its rays,
by those arrows released by Drona's son, falling on every side, the two on the chariot, Krishna and Dhananjaya, were covered.
Then Bharadvaja's son (Ashvatthaman) with hundreds of sharp arrows made those two, Madhava and the Pandava, motionless in the battle.
A cry of "Alas" went up from all, moving and unmoving, seeing the protectors of the moving and unmoving covered with arrows.
Hosts of siddhas and charanas gathered on every side, thinking, "May there be welfare of the worlds today."
Such prowess as Drona's son's as he covered the two Krishnas I have never before seen, O king.
I heard repeatedly in the battle the sound of Drona's son's bow, terrifying to foes, like a lion's roar, O king.
And his bowstring as he ranged in battle, shooting right and left, seemed to shine like lightning in the middle of a cloud.
The Pandava, quick-working and firm-handed, fell into utmost bewilderment and looked at Drona's son.
He thought his valour taken by the great soul, and, O king, in the battle his form became hard to look at.
While the great battle of Drona's son and the Pandava went on, with the mighty son of Drona increasing and the son of Kunti declining, anger came upon Krishna.
Enraged, sighing, O king, as if burning with his eyes, he looked at Drona's son in the battle and at Phalguna again and again.
Then Krishna said, angry and with affection, to Partha: "This is very wondrous, Partha, that I see in battle: Drona's son exceeds you today, O Bharata.
Is Gandiva in your hand? Are you on the chariot, Arjuna? Are your arms well? Is your strength the same?"
Thus addressed by Krishna, hastening, he loosed fourteen broad-headed arrows and in time cut the bow of Drona's son, with his banner, parasol, pennant, chariot, dart and mace.
He struck him hard in the collarbone with calf-tooth arrows; he, falling into deep faintness, leant on the flagstaff.
His charioteer carried him, senseless, afflicted by fear of Kiritin, away from the battle, protecting him from Dhananjaya.
At that very time, Vijaya, tormentor of foes, slew your army by hundreds and thousands, in the sight of your son, the hero, O Bharata.
Thus this destruction of your men by the enemy occurred, cruel, slaughterous, dreadful, O king, through your ill counsel.
The son of Kunti slew the Samshaptakas, Vrikodara the Kurus, and the Panchala Vasushena (Karna) in the battle, in full.

Behind him those led by Dhrishtadyumna are returning—the Panchalas, Srinjayas and Pandavas, who are the front; the great enemy army has been broken by the returned Parthas.
mahabharata:8:41.4	This Karna, Arjuna, holds back the fleeing Kauravas, like Death in speed, like Shakra in prowess.
mahabharata:8:41.5	Over there goes, O Kaurava, Drona's son, best of weapon-bearers; the great chariot-warrior Dhrishtadyumna has rushed at him in the battle.
The unassailable Vasudeva told it all to Kiritin; then, O king, a most dreadful great battle arose.
Lion-roars arose there in the meeting of the two armies, O king, those having made death their return.
Then began the terrible, hair-raising battle of Karna and the Pandavas, increasing the realm of Yama.
When that battle was joined, tumultuous, with water of blood, and a few of the brave Samshaptakas remained, O Bharata,
Dhrishtadyumna, O great king, with all the kings, and the great chariot-warrior Pandavas ran at Karna alone.
Karna alone held in the battle those coming, delighted and eager for victory, as a mountain holds floods of water.
Reaching Karna, those great chariot-warriors were broken like floods reaching a mountain on every side; a hair-raising battle took place between them, O great king.
Dhrishtadyumna struck Radheya with a straight-jointed arrow, enraged, saying "Stand, stand!"
Shaking the excellent bow Vijaya, the great chariot-warrior cut the Parshata's bow and, enraged, struck the Parshata with nine arrows like venomous serpents.
They, piercing that great soul's golden armour, shone, blood-stained, like Indra's cochineal insects, O sinless one.
Casting aside the cut bow, the great chariot-warrior Dhrishtadyumna, taking another bow and arrows like venomous serpents, pierced Karna with seventy straight-jointed arrows.
Likewise, O king, Karna, the mighty archer, pierced the Parshata, scorcher of foes and enemy of Drona, with sharp arrows.
Karna sent at him, O great king, a golden-adorned arrow, enraged, like another rod of Death.
As that dreadful arrow suddenly came, O lord of men, Shaineya cut it in seven, like a skilled one.
Seeing the arrow cut by arrows, Karna, O lord of men, surrounded Satyaki on every side with a shower of arrows.
Ah, time is exceedingly strong, and fate supreme, where all the kings, equal to Shakra in strength, were slain!
Resting for a while, with their best horses having obtained water, they reached a great forest at sunset.
Surely I did some wrong in former births, that the Creator has joined me to deeds that bring sorrow.
There is another matter, Lord Narada, that I shall tell you: through keeping a secret I have been joined to sorrow by Kunti.

There will be no deathlessness when this one is killed; what harm would come of his not being killed, to a person of this creature's life? On his being released, what other man would go to Death's endless world?
Acting equally towards all beings, O lord of men, may all your kinsmen live on you, O increaser of kin.
The Pandavas presented to Dhritarashtra costly garments and many kinds of garlands, as was proper.
By which you, ill-conducted, cruel, filled with wrath, will be exterminators of your whole family, except Rama and Janardana.
Bhima, Arjuna, the twins and the renowned Draupadi, O lord of men, likewise all took garments of bark.
Thus addressed by Narada, the Kuru king Yudhishthira, the wise, asked his brothers and spoke these words.
